Abstract This study investigates the factors influencing the continued use of Islamic mobile banking services in Indonesia, focusing on the role of religiosity and digital literacy within the Expectation Confirmation Model (ECM) framework. Despite technical disruptions, many users continue to use Islamic mobile banking services, raising questions about the underlying drivers of behavior. This study uses a quantitative approach with a survey method. Using purposive sampling, data were collected from 505 Islamic mobile banking users in Indonesia. Data analysis was conducted using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to test the relationship between variables. The results showed that religiosity and Perceived Usefulness significantly influenced user satisfaction. In addition, user satisfaction directly increases IS Continuance Intention, meaning that the more satisfied users are with the service, the higher their intention to continue using it. Furthermore, this study tests the Expectation Confirmation Model (ECM) by integrating religiosity and digital literacy as important external factors, extending its application to Islamic digital services. The research findings show that user values (religiosity) and digital skills (literacy) significantly shape satisfaction and intention to continue beyond technical performance. Further research can explore users' psychological and behavioral aspects that contribute to user decisions in using Islamic mobile banking services in the digital era. Keywords: sharia mobile banking, information system, digital literacy, religiosity, continuance intention 1. Introduction As a country with a Muslim population, Indonesia has great potential in developing Islamic banking services (Zaini et al., 2019), (Wany et al., 2019). One sector that has experienced significant development is Islamic mobile banking (Siregar, 2014). Islamic mobile banking offers easy access and transactions based on Islamic principles, thus attracting more people to use this service to meet their financial needs (Aziz et al., 2023). Islamic banking services recorded asset growth of 15.63% (IDR 802.26 trillion) in 2024, higher than conventional bank assets of 9.5% in the same year (Financial Services Authority, 2024). This growth shows that people are increasingly aware of the importance of financial services guided by religious values, opening up new opportunities for financial institutions to innovate their products and services(Natakusumah et al., 2023). A strong religious background influences people's preference for Sharia services because products that comply with religious principles tend to be more trusted and widely accepted (Ishak et al., 2022; Toumey, 2020). However, implementing Islamic mobile banking is not free from various technical obstacles to mobile banking in Indonesia, such as what happened to the largest Islamic bank with around 15 million customers in Indonesia in May 2023, which disrupted services (Baidhowi, 2018). Improving infrastructure and information technology systems that support Islamic mobile banking services can run more optimally and meet customer expectations regarding transaction speed and security needs to be improved (Zaini et al., 2019). Failure in technology can significantly reduce customer satisfaction with digital services (Putra & Febriati, 2022). Interestingly, most customers continue using the service after the abovementioned disruption, which indicates that other important factors besides technical performance affect the sustainability of Islamic mobile banking users. Understanding post-adoption behavior, especially the intention to continue using the service, is important for the long-term success of Islamic Banks amidst digital service competition (Ramadhan, 2022). Previous research on the sustainability of information system use has shown that user intention to continue using the system is greatly influenced by the level of post-use satisfaction and perceived benefits obtained(Baidhowi, 2018). The Expectation-Confirmation Model (ECM) was developed by Bhattacherjee, which explains that the intention to continue using the system is determined by user satisfaction, which is the result of confirmation of initial expectations and perceptions of post-use system benefits (Prasetya et al., 2022a); (Salem Al-Mamary et al., 2023). Thus, users who experience positive Multidiscip. Sci. J. (2026) 8:e2026135 Accepted: July 13, 2025 Suratno et al. (2026) 2 confirmation of initial expectations tend to have high perceived benefits, which ultimately results in satisfaction and encourages continued use of the information system (Gao & Bai, 2014). On the other hand, in Islamic banking services, additional factors such as religiosity and digital literacy have the potential to influence user satisfaction and loyalty but have not been fully explored in previous studies (Inayah et al., 2018). Research on the sustainability of information system use still focuses on conventional banks and traditional variables of the Technology Acceptance Model and Expectation Confirmation Theory without considering specific aspects such as religiosity, which are very relevant in the context of sharia (Vedadi & Warkentin, 2016). Digital literacy is also an important aspect that has not been comprehensively studied in the context of the sustainability of information system use, especially Islamic mobile banking services, even though this factor influences user adaptation to digital technology (Grefen, 2021). Therefore, this study aims to empirically explore the influence of religiosity and digital literacy on the sustainability of the use of Islamic mobile banking services in Indonesia by integrating these variables in the Expectation-Confirmation model. Specifically, this study empirically tests how confirmation of expectations, perceived benefits, satisfaction, religiosity, and digital literacy influence users' intention to continue using Islamic mobile banking services. 2. Literature Review and Hypothesis Development 2.1. The Influence of Confirmation on Perceived Benefits Confirmation of expectations is a crucial factor that influences users' re-evaluation of the benefits of an information system after initial adoption (Islam, 2011). This evaluation examines how well the system works and how users believe the service meets expectations based on their needs and values (Usman & Projo, 2022). When users of Islamic mobile banking services find that the application's performance meets or exceeds user expectations, such as ease of use of application features and faster transaction access, these users tend to increase their perception of the benefits of the service (Suhartanto et al., 2019). Users will be motivated to continue using the service and recommend it to others, leading to a long-term positive impact on using this technology (Hong et al., 2006), (Gupta et al., 2020). Positive user confirmation significantly strengthens perceived usefulness after users experience the system directly, encouraging users to extend their service use (Hasyim et al., 2022). Users tend to rate a system as more useful when the user experience meets or exceeds their initial expectations, so the stronger the confirmation of expectations, the higher the perceived usefulness felt by users (Gross & Bürglen, 2014). By considering the conceptual relationship and empirical support, this study formulates the following hypothesis: H1: Confirmation of the use of Islamic mobile banking has a positive effect on perceived usefulness. 2.2. The Effect of Confirmation on Satisfaction Confirmation of expectations directly affects user satisfaction with Islamic mobile banking services (Wahid, 2022). When the realization of the service meets or exceeds user expectations, user satisfaction will increase significantly, encouraging users to continue interacting with the system (Wang et al., 2019). High satisfaction not only increases user loyalty but also has the potential to expand service adoption among the Community (Chen, 2012). User satisfaction is the result of evaluating whether the performance of a service meets or exceeds the user's initial expectations (Masrek & Gaskin, 2016). When Islamic mobile banking users find that the services they receive meet or exceed user expectations, such as ease of navigation, transaction speed, and availability of Islamic features, they tend to be satisfied with the service (Cahyani & Utami, 2018). Research by (Bhattacherjee, 2001) shows that confirmation of expectations significantly positively affects user satisfaction with information systems(Zhou, 2013); (Suhartanto et al., 2019). Confirmation of expectations directly increases user satisfaction in the context of digital services (Hossain & Quaddus, 2011). Positive confirmation of expectations contributes significantly to user satisfaction using mobile banking services (Sarabi, 2010) . This study formulates the following hypothesis: H2: Confirmation of the use of Islamic mobile banking has a positive effect on user satisfaction. 2.3. The Influence of Perceived Benefits on Satisfaction Perceived usefulness is an important determinant of user satisfaction in mobile banking (Wahid, 2022).When users believe that the service is helpful in their daily activities, satisfaction increases (Aman & Smith-Colin, 2022); (Lee & Shim, 2007). In addition to being influenced by confirmation, user satisfaction is also influenced by cognitive evaluation of the perceived benefits of the servisse (Chatterjee & Moitra, 2022). In mobile banking services, customers who feel the application is practical and provides real added value tend to be more satisfied with their user experience (Shaikh & Karjaluoto, 2015). (Bhattacherjee, 2001) found that post-use perceived usefulness positively affects user satisfaction (Ohk et al., 2015); (Saeed & Abdinnour- Helm, 2008). Similar findings have been widely reported in previous technology adoption studies, where perceived benefits or performance are determinants of customer satisfaction in mobile banking (Shrestha, 2020); (Ghimire & Dhakal, 2023). Therefore, this study formulates the following hypothesis: H3: The perceived usefulness of Islamic mobile banking positively affects user satisfaction. 2.4. Users continue using services that provide tangible benefits for daily activities, such as ease and efficiency of transactions (Susanti & Alamsyah, 2022); (Liu & Wang, 2023). In addition to encouraging initial adoption, banks must ensure that users have a strong reason to continue using technology services (Bureshaid et al., 2022). User satisfaction is an important indicator in the sustainability of technology service use (Araújo et al., 2021). Post-use satisfaction can shape the intention to continue using information systems (Mishra et al., 2023). Satisfaction reflects the user's affective evaluation of how well the service meets user expectations (Yu & Davis, 2024). Previous studies have shown a positive and significant relationship between satisfaction and continuance intention in various digital services (Kumar et al., 2020). Satisfaction is an important mediator that bridges the perception of value to loyalty in using digital financial services; satisfied users are more likely to continue using them because they feel safe, comfortable, and get the benefits they expect (Kar, 2020). Satisfaction comes from the functional aspects of technology and the extent to which the service reflects the Shari (Zouari & Abdelhedi, 2021) lieve (Zouari & Abdelhedi, 2021). Users who are satisfied with both the functional and technical sides tend to have a stronger emotional connection with the services they use, thus strengthening them to continue using technology services sustainably, even when minor technical problems occur (Calvo-Porral et al., 2016). The higher the user satisfaction with mobile banking services, the higher the intention to continue using the service (Huseynli et al., 2023). Therefore, this study formulates the following hypothesis: H5: Satisfaction positively affects the continuance intention of using Islamic mobile banking. 2.6. The Influence of Religiosity on Continuance Intention Religiosity is how individuals internalize and practice their religious values daily (Iddagoda & Opatha, 2018). In Islamic banking, customer religiosity plays an important role because Islamic services emerge as an alternative by Islamic financial principles (Das, 2012; Permana et al., 2022). For highly religious customers, bank compliance with Islamic principles can be a factor of satisfaction beyond the service's functional aspects(Tegambwage & Kasoga, 2023). Previous studies have shown that higher levels of religiosity correlate with increased customer satisfaction and loyalty in Islamic banks (Riptiono et al., 2021). The stronger the religiosity of the customer, the higher the user satisfaction with Islamic banking services (Mohd Dali et al., 2014). Customers with high religiosity tend to appreciate the Islamic values fulfilled by Islamic banks, so even if technical obstacles occur, users may be more patient or tolerant as long as Islamic principles are guaranteed. Religiosity can also directly drive continuance intention (Kamarozaman & Zaidi, 2021). Users who hold firm to Islamic values may continue to use Islamic mobile banking because they consider switching to a conventional bank less in line with their principles (Inayah et al., 2018). The positive and significant influence of religiosity drives consumer intentions to use Islamic mobile banking (Sudarsono et al., 2022). Trust and attitudes towards Islamic banks are greatly influenced by the level of religiosity, which ultimately increases the intention to choose Islamic banking services (Permana et al., 2022). In other words, spiritual values drive customer continuity in Islamic mobile banking (Rahayu, 2018). Users feel a moral obligation or strong preference to continue using halal and sharia-compliant products (Ghazali et al., 2022). Based on this literature, this study positions religiosity as an external factor influencing satisfaction and continued intention. Based on the description above, the following hypothesis is formulated. H6: Customer religiosity positively affects the continuance intention to use Islamic mobile banking. 2.7. The Influence of Digital Literacy on Continuance Intention Digital literacy can be defined as an individual's knowledge and skills in using digital technology effectively (Grefen, 2021). In the mobile banking framework, digital literacy includes customers' understanding of applications, cybersecurity, digital financial features, and the ability to solve simple technical problems (Suhartanto et al., 2019). High digital literacy usually makes users more confident and adaptable to digital banking services, reducing stress when facing obstacles (Bosanac & Luić, 2021). Conversely, customers with low digital literacy may quickly feel difficulty or worry when errors occur, reducing satisfaction and intention to continue using (Vollbrecht et al., 2020). Digital literacy is critical in determining customer https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Suratno et al. (2026) 4 experience using information systems (mounaim et al., 2022). Digital literacy directly increases adoption and consumer satisfaction using electronic banking services (Amini et al., 2020). Digital literacy significantly positively affects customer satisfaction and continued intention to use mobile financial services (Ullah et al., 2022). The higher the customer's technological understanding and skills, the more optimally the user utilizes the service, which leads to higher satisfaction, and ultimately encourages continued use of mobile banking (Özecan & ARıkan, 2022). Based on the description above, the following hypothesis is formulated. H7: Digital literacy positively affects the continuance intention to use Islamic mobile banking. 2.8. Satisfaction mediates the relationship between perceived benefits and continued intention User satisfaction is an important mediating factor that strengthens the relationship between perceived benefits and continuance intention to use Islamic mobile banking (Chan et al., 2022). When users feel real benefits from the service, user satisfaction increases, which ultimately increases the user's intention to continue using the servisse (Kar, 2020). Satisfaction plays a vital role in bridging perceived benefits with continuance intention, because satisfied users tend to be more loyal and highly committed to continue using the servisse (Abror et al., 2021). Satisfaction, in turn, increases the user's intention to continue using the servisse (Araújo et al., 2021). Perceived benefits positively affect satisfaction, impacting continuance intention (Hsieh, 2018). Satisfaction mediates the relationship between perceived usefulness and intention to continue using mobile banking (Foroughi et al., 2019). User satisfaction mediates between perceived usefulness and continuance intention in mobile banking applications (Özecan & ARıkan, 2022). Satisfaction is a significant mediation pathway in the Expectation Confirmation Model (Asnakew, 2020). Based on the above description, the following hypotheses are formulated. H8: Satisfaction mediates the relationship between perceived usefulness and intention to continue using Islamic mobile banking. 2.9. Satisfaction mediates between confirmation and continued intention Users who feel their expectations are met tend to have a high level of satisfaction, thus giving rise to a firm intention to continue using the service in the long term (Tang et al., 2022). When users find that the service received meets or exceeds initial expectations regarding transaction speed, ease of navigation, and availability of Sharia features, users tend to be satisfied with the service provided (Wahyoedi et al., 2021). Confirmation of expectations significantly affects user satisfaction with information systems (Bhattacherjee, 2001; Hossain & Quaddus, 2011). Confirmation of expectations directly increases user satisfaction in the context of digital services (Kumar et al., 2020). User satisfaction mediates between expectation confirmation and continuance intention in mobile banking applications (Özecan & ARıkan, 2022). Satisfaction significantly mediates between expectation confirmation and continuance intention (Amin et al., 2014). Based on the description above, the following hypothesis is formulated. The research design used is causal explanatory research, where the independent variables (confirmation, https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Suratno et al. The research instrument is a structured questionnaire consisting of several main parts. The first part contains basic demographic questions (age, gender, education, length of use of Islamic mobile banking, and frequency of use per week). The next part contains statements to measure each research variable. The measurement scale assesses the extent to which the subject agrees or disagrees with the question. The variables to be measured are described as a reference for formulating question items, where the direction of the question to the right indicates stronger agreement (SS), which indicates a higher level of agreement. Conversely, if the direction of the assessment moves to the left, this indicates increasingly strong disagreement (STS), which means a higher level of rejection. The scale used in this study uses a five-point Likert scale, namely (1) strongly disagree, (2) disagree, (3) quite agree, (4) agree, and (5) strongly agree. The initial step before distributing the questionnaire to respondents was a pilot test conducted on 30 respondents to ensure the questions' clarity and the instrument's reliability. The primary purpose of implementing the pilot test is to evaluate the effectiveness of the survey instrument that will be distributed to respondentes (Sugiyono, 2014). From the instrument test results, it was stated that 18 measurement items in the study were declared valid. The study population consisted of users of Islamic mobile banking in Indonesia. Given the vast population, the sampling technique chosen was purposive sampling with the following respondent criteria: (a) are Islamic bank customers who actively use Islamic mobile banking applications, and (b) have used mobile banking at least 5 times in the last 1 month. The second criterion is designed to ensure that respondents have sufficient experience with the system to provide meaningful reflections on their interactions with it. To strengthen the representativeness of the sample, we ensured geographic diversity by targeting users from different regions. As a result, the respondents in this study came from 29 provinces across Indonesia, providing a broad and diverse demographic base that supports the contextual relevance of the findings. A total of 505 responses were successfully collected over a one-month survey period. The questionnaire was distributed online via Google Forms and disseminated through various social media platforms, including WhatsApp, Instagram, and TikTok. The online survey approach was chosen because mobile banking users are typically digitally literate and active internet users, making online distribution more accessible and practical (Motiwalla et al., 2018). Assessment of Measurement Model The collected data were analyzed using the Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) method based on covariance. The analysis tool used is SmartPLS 4.0 software. SEM was chosen because it is suitable for testing simultaneous relationships between many latent variables and indicators. The analysis in this study was carried out in two main stages. The first stage evaluates the measurement model, which aims to test the validity and reliability of the indicators used to measure latent variables. The measurement model ensures that each indicator truly reflects the concept to be measured and does not experience reliability problems (Hair et al., 2018) . The second stage evaluates the structural model, which aims to test the hypothesis and causal relationships between latent variables (Sarstedt et al., 2021). Validity and reliability tests are used to evaluate the measurement quality in the Partial Least Squares (PLS)-based structural model. Validity consists of convergent validity and discriminant validity. Convergent validity shows how closely the relationship is between indicators in one construct, which is evaluated through the loading factor value (> 0.7 for confirmatory research and 0.6–0.7 is still acceptable for exploratory research) and the Average Variance Extracted (AVE) value must be greater than 0.5 (Hair et al., 2018). Good discriminant validity can be shown if the square root of the AVE of each construct is greater than the correlation between constructs, and the cross-loading value of each indicator is higher against its construct compared to other constructs(Fornell & Larcker, 1981); (Hair et al., 2018). Reliability tests are used to measure the internal consistency of a construct in a research instrument. The two methods used are Cronbach's Alpha and Composite Reliability. Cronbach's Alpha is used to assess minimum reliability, with a value of ≥ 0.7 considered good, although a value of ≥ 0.6 is still acceptable in exploratory studies (Hair et al., 2018). Table 3 shows adequate loading values above 0.7, indicating that each item significantly contributes to measuring the construct. Although there is one DL33 indicator with a loading value of 0.647, which is slightly below the ideal threshold of 0.7, this indicator still contributes positively to the AVE value and composite reliability, so DL33 can still be maintained in the model (Hair et al., 2018). Discussion This study shows user satisfaction strongly influences the intention to continue using Islamic mobile banking services. When the service experience matches or exceeds initial expectations, users feel satisfied and continue using the application. Several recent studies place satisfaction as the primary determinant in the sustainability of digital system use, including in the financial sector, where, when the system has a uniqueness based on religious values, the post-adoption mechanism is still influenced by the user's affective evaluation of the usage experience. (Alalwan et al., 2017; Ofori et al., 2016). These findings support the Expectation-Confirmation Model (ECM) framework developed by (Bhattacherjee, 2001), where the expectation confirmation process plays an important role in shaping satisfaction and driving continuation intentions. These results are also consistent with the study of (Wu, 2017), which found that satisfaction acts as a mediator between confirmation, perceived usefulness, and continuation intentions in digital payment services. User satisfaction increases when their expectations of the digital platform are met (Siddiqui et al., 2019). The contribution of confirmation to satisfaction and perceived usefulness in the research reaffirms the importance of expectation management in implementing digital services (Bhattacherjee, 2001). When users feel that the experience delivers what is promised, positive evaluations are formed in layers, covering functional and spiritual aspects (Inayah et al., 2018). Studies by (Oghuma et al., 2015; Prasetya et al., 2022b) also found that high expectation confirmation increases perceived value and satisfaction in value-based digital services. Therefore, the success of the sharia system lies not only in technical capabilities but also in the ability to convey Islamic values consistently. Although perceived usefulness is not as strong as satisfaction in influencing continuance intention, users process benefits rationally in decision making. Research conducted by (Kanungo, 2022) shows that users of digital financial services assess utility not only from a technical perspective, but also from a compliance with value norms. One of the strongest conceptual contributions of this study is the role of religiosity. This study shows that religiosity significantly indirectly affects continuance intention through satisfaction. This finding strengthens the literature that places religiosity as a cognitive and affective driver in evaluating the Sharia system (Fatmawati et al., 2024). The concept of value congruence becomes relevant where users feel satisfied because they find a match between personal values (faith) and institutional values (Sharia principles). Satisfaction is rational but emotional and spiritual, substantially strengthening the sustainability of use. From the perspective of user-specific characteristics, the digital literacy dimension is an additional key in explaining the variability of continued use (Sabila & Hasnawati, 2024). This study proves that digital literacy affects the perception of benefits and increases user satisfaction. This perspective aligns with the literature on technology readiness and self-efficacy, emphasizing that technological competence is a significant prerequisite for adopting and sustaining digital systems (Uddin & Nasrin, 2023). In addition, digital literacy is also correlated with innovation diffusion theory, especially in the confirmation and decision phases, where individuals with high literacy are quicker to adopt and maintain the use of technology (Shareef et al., 2018). This study provides a new direction for developing information system sustainability models by emphasizing that the success of digital services, especially in the sharia sector, is primarily determined by the suitability of values, user capabilities, https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Suratno et al. (2026) 12 and system quality. Integration of technical constructs (satisfaction, usefulness, confirmation), socio-religious dimensions (religiosity), and user competence factors (digital literacy) in one conceptual framework. This finding confirms that the basic principles of ECM remain relevant when applied in services based on religious values, such as Sharia mobile banking. Although this service contains spiritual elements, user satisfaction is still determined by evaluating cognitive and emotional experiences. This study expands the application of ECM into a more complex and value-based context. It shows that the experience-based and expectation-based approaches are still very relevant in explaining the behavior of digital technology users today. 6. Implications and Future Research This study provides several important implications, both theoretically and practically. From a theoretical perspective, the findings broaden the scope of the Expectation-Confirmation Model (ECM) by incorporating two contextual variables, namely religiosity and digital literacy, into the sustainability of technology use. The results show that religiosity can influence satisfaction and continuance intention, indicating the need to expand the ECM theoretical framework to accommodate sociocultural dimensions, especially in value-based services such as Islamic banking. In addition, the contribution of digital literacy to user satisfaction and loyalty supports a more inclusive and responsive approach to individual user characteristics in information system models. From a practical perspective, the results of this study suggest that Islamic financial institutions need to seriously consider two strategic approaches: (1) strengthening the religious dimension in digital services that are tailored to Islamic values believed by users, such as transparency, ease of worship, and guarantee of compliance with sharia principles; and (2) increasing digital literacy for customers, through education, application usage guides, and basic technology training that is easily accessible. Both approaches are believed to strengthen user satisfaction and encourage long-term loyalty to Sharia-based digital services. Although the results of this study provide significant contributions to the development of theories and practices of sustainable information system use, several limitations can be opportunities for further research agendas. First, this study is limited to Islamic mobile banking users in Indonesia. Future research can expand the geographical scope by comparing users from different countries or cultural backgrounds to test the generalizability of the developed model. Second, this research approach is quantitative and survey-based; further exploration through qualitative or mixed-method approaches can further explore user motivations and perceptions. 7. Conclusions This study provides strong empirical evidence that the continuance of Islamic mobile banking services is determined by the interaction between technical aspects, religious values, and users' digital capacity. Satisfaction emerges as a key factor that shapes the intention to continue using, which is reinforced by positive experiences based on expectations (confirmation ) and perceptions of the functional benefits of the system (perceived usefulness ). These findings confirm the relevance of the Expectation-Confirmation Model (ECM) in digital banking and extend its application to spiritual value-based services, proving that user satisfaction is the primary foundation in creating long-term sustainability of information technology use. Religiosity has been proven to increase user satisfaction effectively and significantly. Religious values are not only normative preferences but are intrinsic elements that influence user perceptions, evaluations, and decisions in Islamic banking. Religiosity encourages loyalty to services despite technical disruptions because users feel bound by the suitability of values between themselves and the bank's operational principles. The sustainability of using a Sharia-based system is not built solely on system performance but also on the depth of values the service accommodates. The role of digital literacy is to strengthen the user's capacity to navigate and utilize the system optimally. Digital literacy acts as an enabler that increases satisfaction and sustainability while also being a reminder that the success of financial technology services also depends on user readiness. Therefore, financial institutions need to adopt a holistic approach focusing on functional excellence, Sharia compliance, and user empowerment through increased digital literacy in designing a strategy for developing Islamic mobile banking services. Islamic banks can build a solid foundation for sustainability in a competitive and dynamic digital financial services ecosystem by integrating the three main pillars of satisfaction, religious values, and digital capabilities. JSON: Name: ecm_sharia_mobile_continuance Title: PLS-SEM survey analysis of religiosity and digital literacy effects on continuance intention of sharia mobile banking in Indonesia Short Hypothesis: Higher user religiosity and higher digital literacy cause increased continuance intention to use sharia mobile banking, mediated by higher perceived usefulness and greater user satisfaction. Related Work: Prior work primarily applies the Expectation-Confirmation Model (ECM) and Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to predict continuance intention in digital banking; extensions add trust, service quality, or demographic moderators. Separate streams study religiosity as a driver of preference for sharia products and digital literacy as an enabler of technology adoption. Limitations include (1) narrow focus on conventional banking or single-factor extensions rather than jointly modeling religiosity and digital literacy within ECM, (2) heavy reliance on cross-sectional surveys without robust mediation and predictive checks, (3) limited discriminant validity and common-method control in many studies, (4) under-reporting of model ablation/robustness checks and multigroup invariance, and (5) geographically constrained samples or demographic skews that limit generalizability. Abstract: This study addresses the determinants of continued use of sharia (Islamic) mobile banking by integrating religiosity and digital literacy into the Expectation-Confirmation Model (ECM). We propose a quantitative survey-based approach with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to test whether religiosity and digital literacy increase continuance intention via perceived usefulness and satisfaction. The primary contribution is an empirically validated, extended ECM that quantifies direct and mediated paths from religiosity and digital literacy to continuance intention and compares model variants using ablation and predictive validity tests. Expected outcomes include effect-size estimates, explained variance (R2) for satisfaction and continuance intention, and evidence on whether adding religiosity and digital literacy significantly improves predictive performance over standard ECM. Results will inform measurement validity of value-based and capability constructs in post-adoption models and clarify the relative contribution of socio-religious versus technical competence factors to digital financial service sustainability. Experiments: Dataset: target N >= 500 completed responses from active sharia mobile banking users in Indonesia; inclusion criteria: Muslim account holders who used the app >=5 times in last month; geographic coverage across provinces; holdout split: 80% train / 20% test for predictive validation; optional external replication sample N >= 200 from a different time window. Questionnaire: multi-item Likert (1–5) scales for Confirmation (3 items), Perceived Usefulness (3), Satisfaction (3), Religiosity (3), Digital Literacy (3), Continuance Intention (3); pilot N=30 for item tuning. Baselines: (A) standard ECM (Confirmation -> PU -> Satisfaction -> Continuance Intention), (B) TAM-based model (PU, PEOU -> Intention), (C) reduced ECM without religiosity, (D) reduced ECM without digital literacy. Primary model: full extended ECM estimated via PLS-SEM. Robustness models: covariance-based SEM (lavaan) on same data. Evaluation metrics: path coefficient estimates with bootstrapped t-values and p-values (bootstrap resamples = 5,000), R2 for Satisfaction and Continuance Intention, effect size f2 for each predictor, Q2 (PLS blindfolding) for predictive relevance, SRMR for model fit, AVE and Composite Reliability for measurement validity, HTMT < 0.90 for discriminant validity, common-method bias tests (Harman single-factor, marker variable). Predictive validation: PLSpredict (10-fold CV) and out-of-sample RMSE comparison between full model and baselines on holdout. Ablation study: compute ΔR2 and change in predictive RMSE when removing religiosity, removing digital literacy, and removing both; report significance of ΔR2 via permutation or nested-model bootstrapping. Multigroup analysis: test path invariance across gender, age groups, and main bank (BSI vs others) with permutation tests. Reporting: standardized coefficients, 95% confidence intervals, p-values, f2, Q2, SRMR, AVE, CR, HTMT, out-of-sample RMSE and comparative tables for baselines and ablations. Risk Factors and Limitations: Self-report and social desirability bias in religiosity and satisfaction measures; common-method variance due to single-source cross-sectional survey; sample demographic skew (e.g., overrepresentation of students and females) limiting representativeness; cross-sectional design restricts causal inference and temporal stability of continuance intention; construct measurement validity risk for religiosity and digital literacy across subpopulations; potential omitted-variable bias (e.g., trust, service outages, pricing) confounding estimated effects; limited external generalizability beyond Indonesian sharia banking context; PLS-SEM sensitivity to indicator reliability and small effect sizes producing unstable estimates for weak paths; nonresponse and selection bias from online distribution channels; multicollinearity between related constructs reducing interpretability of individual path coefficients.
